label: sec:exp
title: Reasoning about Integer Exponentiation
html:
In our integration into cvc5, we generalize the operator pow2​ of [7] to exp, the integer exponentiation operator ** of the SMT-LIB theory of integers, and translate pow2​(k) to exp(2,k).

4.1 Semantics

The operator exp has arity Int×Int→Int. We use the semantics of ** in the SMT-LIB theory of integers [4]. For a non-negative exponent t≥0, exp(s,t) is s to the power of t, and in particular exp(0,0)=1. For a negative exponent t<0, exp is defined so as to satisfy exp(s,t)=1divexp(s,−t) whenever the div term is defined, and the following holds for all t<0: exp(0,t)=0,exp(s,t)=exp(s,−t) if ∣s∣=1,exp(s,t)=0 if ∣s∣>1. In other words, since we follow the convention exp(0,0)=1, exp(s,t) is s to the power of t whenever this is an integer, and 0 otherwise.

SwInE [14] interprets exp(s,t) as s∣t∣ instead. Since st is not an integer for t<0 and ∣s∣>1, exponentiation is intuitively a partial function on the integers, but all functions are total in SMT-LIB logic. SwInE resolves this by taking the absolute value of the exponent, a semantics that keeps laws of exponentiation such as exp(exp(x,y),z)=exp(x,y⋅z) valid. The two semantics agree on non-negative exponents, but differ on negative ones, e.g., exp(2,−1) is 2 in SwInE and 0 under the SMT-LIB semantics.

4.2 Rewriting

Table 2 lists the rewrite rules for exp-terms. These rules are written in RARE and compiled into the rewriter of cvc5 (Section 3). We use a script to generate from the RARE files both the LaTeX rewrite tables of this paper (such as Table 2) and the statements of their Lean soundness theorems (see Section 6), so that the implemented rules, the rules in the paper and the rules proved sound are the same. From SwInE [14], we take the rewrite rules that are sound under our semantics, i.e., the rules with source [14] in Table 2. The rewrite rules only handle non-negative exponents, and negative exponents are left to the lemmas of the CEGAR loop (Section 4.3). The other rules of SwInE are not applied as rewrites. In particular, the composition rule exp(exp(x,y),z)→exp(x,y⋅z) is unsound under the SMT-LIB semantics (for x=y=z=−6, the left-hand side is exp(0,−6)=0, while the right-hand side is (−6)36), and is therefore realized as the guarded lemma compose of Table 3.

4.3 Lemmas for the CEGAR Loop

Table 3 lists the lemmas of the exp-solver for the refinement in the CEGAR loop. The lemmas of our exp-solver combine the pow2​-lemmas of [7], generalized from base 2 to an arbitrary base s, the lemma families of SwInE [14], and new lemmas motivated by translated TPBV​-formulas. Our solver handles negative exponents by the semantics of Section 4.1: lemma neg-def of Table 3 expresses exp(s,t) for t<0 by 1divexp(s,−t), parity-minus-one fixes the value of exp(−1,t), and the other cases are left to lemma value. We take many useful lemmas from SwInE [14]. Since SwInE interprets exp(s,t) as s∣t∣, some of its lemmas for negative exponents do not hold under our semantics, and we omit them. For example, the symmetry lemma sym3​, exp(s,t)=exp(s,−t), of SwInE is unsound under the SMT-LIB semantics, so we use it only for ∣s∣≤1, where it holds. For other lemmas, we add the guards that they need under our semantics, e.g., the composition lemma of SwInE becomes compose, y≥0∧z≥0⇒exp(exp(x,y),z)=exp(x,y⋅z). Without the guards, the lemma is unsound under the SMT-LIB semantics, since negative exponents do not multiply: for x=2 and y=z=−1, the left-hand side is exp(exp(2,−1),−1)=exp(0,−1)=0, while the right-hand side is exp(2,1)=2. The lemmas value, induction and the interpolation lemmas are instantiated with values of the candidate model, and we use the notation of SwInE [14] for them. In Table 3, v and w are variables that are instantiated with the model values sI and tI, respectively, and d is instantiated as indicated. exp(s,t)I is the value of the term exp(s,t) in I, where exp is uninterpreted. Thus, the side condition exp(s,t)I>vw of interpolate-upper (resp. exp(s,t)I<vw of interpolate-lower) states that I overestimates (resp. underestimates) the power vw, and the lemma is only instantiated in that case. In interpolate-upper, [c−,c+]×[d−,d+] is the smallest box containing (v,w) and a previously used interpolation point, the lemma is only instantiated if c−≥0 and d−≥0, and ip[c−,c+][d−,d+](x,y) denotes the bilinear interpolant of xy over that box, as defined in SwInE: the linear interpolant of xy along the exponent is ip2[d±]​(x,y):=xd−+d+−d−xd+−xd−​⋅(y−d−), and ip[c−,c+][d−,d+](x,y) interpolates ip2[d±]​(c−,y) and ip2[d±]​(c+,y) linearly in the same way along the base, i.e., between x=c− and x=c+. The lemmas of SwInE are linear, whereas we also add non-linear lemmas that relate powers by divisibility, such as mod-base and divisible. Lemma divisible, (s1​≈s2​∧0<exp(s1​,t1​)≤exp(s2​,t2​))⇒exp(s2​,t2​)modexp(s1​,t1​)≈0, is important for translated TPBV​-formulas, since the translation produces a mod by exp(2,k) for every arithmetic operation at width k. In multi-width formulas, these mod operations are nested with different widths, e.g., (xmodexp(2,m))modexp(2,k) with k≤m, and divisible, which states that exp(2,k) divides exp(2,m), allows the solver to relate them.

For satisfiable formulas, the lemmas are complemented by the phasing technique of SwInE [14], which first searches for models with exponents of small absolute value. The only difference is that we apply all violated lemmas at once, without a precedence among them. For more details, see Appendix B.

Extended: Appendix B. Phasing

For satisfiable formulas, the lemmas are complemented by phasing [14], shown in Algorithm 1. Even when a model with exponents of small absolute value exists, the arithmetic solver often returns candidate models with exponents of large absolute value. Then interpolation lemmas with huge coefficients are generated, since these coefficients grow exponentially in the exponent, and afterwards the solver takes too long to find a new candidate model. Phasing prefers small models over large ones by alternating between a sat-phase and an unsat-phase. In the sat-phase, the goal is to find small candidate models, so the absolute values of the exponents of all relevant exp-terms are bounded by 2b for a level b (Line 9). If no candidate model is found in the sat-phase, the algorithm switches to the unsat-phase (Line 21). In the unsat-phase, the goal is to prove unsatisfiability, so no bound is imposed on the exponents (Line 10). If this fails, the candidate model is discarded without refinement, unless it is a model of φ (Line 13), and the algorithm returns to the sat-phase (Line 14) with a higher level (Line 15). Since the bound 2b grows exponentially in the number of phase changes, the considered models grow rapidly if no small model exists, so that a model can still be found quickly. Unlike [14], which first computes symmetry, monotonicity, bounding and prime lemmas and only resorts to induction and interpolation lemmas if none of them is violated, we compute all violated lemmas of Section 4.3 at once (Line 17). In cvc5, we implement phasing inside the exp-solver: for every exp-term exp(s,t) and level b, we introduce a fresh Boolean guard gb​ and the lemma gb​⇔(−2b≤t∧t≤2b), and instruct the SAT solver to decide gb​ positively first.
